# Boiler Service 2026

## Summary

The 2026 service fell on 19 March, a spring visit that I moved forward after noticing a drip in the airing cupboard. The booking was made about three weeks earlier, and the engineer was on site for fifty-five minutes from the moment he rang the bell. He put the case off, worked through the burner and the water side, and then spent most of his time on the drip that had prompted the call. Everything was written onto the benchmark sheet and signed before he left, and the reminder card went back inside the door for next spring. The visit cost the usual amount plus the price of the new part, which he had on the van and did not need to order. I had left the boiler running so he could watch it fire and then cool, and the drip showed itself within the first ten minutes. The airing cupboard is dry now, and the faint stain on the shelf below the pipe is fading as it dries out. I kept the old part so I could see the corrosion for myself, and the spindle is rough enough that it would never have seated cleanly again.

## Findings

The pressure relief valve had a weeping seat and a corroded spindle. That was the whole of the fault, and once the case was off it was easy to see the trace of water running down from the outlet rather than spraying, which is what a badly failed valve does. The spindle had rusted to the point where it no longer moved smoothly on its seat, so the valve was passing a steady trickle even when the system was nowhere near its limit. The seat itself was marked where the spindle had been sitting out of true, and no amount of cleaning would have brought it back. The rest of the unit was in good order. The burner lit cleanly, the flame was steady and blue through the sight glass, and the case seals were still soft with no cracking at the folds. The magnetic filter had only a light coating of sludge, which he cleaned and refitted. There was no sign of scale in the water passages he could see and no weeping at any of the joints he could reach with a spanner. He said the valve had probably been passing for weeks before it showed, which is why the stain was so faint and slow to appear. The discharge pipe told the same story, with a dry line of scale marking where the water had been running and drying rather than pouring.

## Actions

A new pressure relief valve was fitted in place of the old one, with a fresh washer and the outlet sealed properly onto the pipe. The discharge pipe was re-run so that it falls away from the wall along its whole length and discharges where a dribble can be seen, since the old run had a slight rise in it that would have hidden a leak. The inhibitor was topped up while the system was open, and he told me to run the heating as normal rather than doing anything special. He asked me to watch the system for a week, checking the gauge cold each morning and looking at the end of the discharge pipe, and to ring him if either showed a change. Everything went back together, the benchmark sheet was signed, and the card for next spring went inside the door. So far the gauge has held steady. I checked the end of the discharge pipe each morning for the first week and found nothing but a dry stain, which is exactly what I wanted to see.
